questions.question: How do you implement Fibonacci in Go — iterative vs recursive?
questions.title: Fibonacci Iterative Recursive
questions.direct_answer: Iterative: loop with two variables (a, b) — O(n), O(1) space, the right answer. Recursive: fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) — O(2^n) exponential, the naive trap that interviews test. Memoization bridges.

Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F5[fib 5] --> F4[fib 4] --> F3[fib 3] --> F2A[fib 2]
    F4 --> F2B[fib 2]
    F5 --> F3B[fib 3]
    F2A --> X1[recomputed]
    F2B --> X2[recomputed]
    style X1 fill:#f99
    style X2 fill:#f99
    ITER[iterative: a,b advance] → N[O n time, O 1 space]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The call-tree arithmetic, concretely: fibRec(n) spawns fibRec(n-1) and fibRec(n-2) — the tree's node count grows as the Fibonacci sequence itself (fib(n) calls ≈ fib(n+1)). fib(40) is ~102 million calls; fib(50) is ~12 billion. The exponential is the worst-case branching factor (2^depth), pruned only by overlapping subtrees.

The memoization's transformation: each memo hit collapses a subtree to an O(1) lookup. The recursion still descends, but each unique n computes once — O(n) unique calls, O(n) map space. The cached form IS the iterative solution wearing a recursive shape.

The tail-recursion note for honesty: Go doesn't optimize tail calls — the iterative loop is not equivalent to a tail-recursive form. The recursive Fibonacci at fibRec(1000) would stack-overflow before it finishes; the iterative runs in microseconds. 'Recursion for shape, iteration for production' is the Go discipline.
